title: Period Basics: Understanding Your Menstrual Cycle
summary: Learn about the four phases of the menstrual cycle, what's typical, and how to track your period effectively.
content:
What is a menstrual cycle?

The menstrual cycle is the monthly process your body goes through to prepare for pregnancy. It typically lasts between 21 and 35 days, with the average being about 28 days.

The Four Phases

1. Menstruation (Days 1-5)

This is when you have your period. The uterine lining sheds, causing bleeding that typically lasts 3-7 days. Flow can vary from light to heavy.

2. Follicular Phase (Days 1-13)

Your body prepares an egg for release. Estrogen levels rise, and you may feel more energetic.

3. Ovulation (Day 14)

An egg is released from the ovary. This is when you're most fertile. Some people notice mild cramping or changes in cervical mucus.

4. Luteal Phase (Days 15-28)

The body prepares for a potential pregnancy. If the egg isn't fertilized, hormone levels drop and PMS symptoms may appear.

Tracking Tips

  • Note the first day of your period each month
  • Track flow intensity (light, medium, heavy)
  • Record any symptoms you experience
  • Look for patterns over 3-6 months

Remember: Every body is different. Your cycle may not be exactly 28 days, and that's perfectly normal.

title: What's Normal vs. Unusual: When to Pay Attention
summary: Understanding the difference between normal cycle variations and signs that may warrant a visit to your healthcare provider.
content:
Normal Variations

Your cycle can vary from month to month. Here are some things that are generally considered normal:

  • Cycle length between 21-35 days
  • Period lasting 3-7 days
  • Mild cramps during the first 1-2 days
  • Slight mood changes before your period
  • Light spotting between periods occasionally
  • Changes in flow from cycle to cycle

When to Consider Seeing a Provider

While many variations are normal, some changes may be worth discussing with a healthcare provider:

  • Periods lasting longer than 7 days consistently
  • Soaking through a pad or tampon every hour for several hours
  • Severe pain that interferes with daily activities
  • Bleeding between periods regularly
  • No period for 3 or more months (if not pregnant)
  • Sudden changes in your usual pattern

Keeping Track

Recording your symptoms and cycle details can help your healthcare provider better understand your situation. Use Bloom's calendar and logging features to keep an organized record.

This information is educational and not a substitute for professional medical advice.

title: PCOS Overview: What You Should Know
summary: A beginner-friendly overview of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome, common symptoms, and how it may affect your cycle.
content:
What is PCOS?

Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is a common hormonal condition that affects people with ovaries. It occurs in about 1 in 10 women of reproductive age.

Common Signs

  • Irregular periods or missed periods
  • Excess hair growth on face or body
  • Acne or oily skin
  • Weight changes
  • Thinning hair on the scalp
  • Difficulty getting pregnant

How It May Affect Your Cycle

PCOS can cause irregular ovulation, which means your periods may be unpredictable. Some people with PCOS have very long cycles (over 35 days), while others may skip periods entirely.

What You Can Do

  • Track your cycle to identify patterns
  • Maintain a balanced diet and regular exercise
  • Speak with a healthcare provider for proper evaluation
  • Consider seeing a specialist (endocrinologist or gynecologist)

Important: PCOS is manageable with proper support. If you suspect you may have PCOS, please consult with a healthcare professional for proper diagnosis and treatment options.

title: Endometriosis: Understanding the Basics
summary: Learn about endometriosis, its common symptoms, and why early awareness matters.
content:
What is Endometriosis?

Endometriosis is a condition where tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus. It affects roughly 10% of reproductive-age women worldwide.

Common Symptoms

  • Painful periods (dysmenorrhea) that may worsen over time
  • Pain during or after intercourse
  • Pain with bowel movements or urination during periods
  • Heavy bleeding or bleeding between periods
  • Fatigue, especially during periods
  • Digestive issues during menstruation

Why Awareness Matters

Endometriosis often takes years to diagnose because its symptoms can be mistaken for normal period pain. Being aware of the signs can help you seek care sooner.

Seeking Help

If you experience severe menstrual pain that limits your activities, consider speaking with a healthcare provider. Keeping a detailed log of your symptoms, their severity, and when they occur can be very helpful for your provider.

This information is educational. Diagnosis requires medical evaluation by a qualified healthcare professional.

title: Menopause & Perimenopause: What to Expect
summary: A guide to understanding the transition to menopause, common symptoms, and ways to find comfort.
content:
What is Perimenopause?

Perimenopause is the transitional period before menopause. It can begin in your 40s (sometimes earlier) and last several years. During this time, your body gradually produces less estrogen.

What is Menopause?

Menopause is confirmed when you've gone 12 consecutive months without a period. The average age is 51, but it can happen earlier or later.

Common Perimenopause Symptoms

  • Irregular periods (shorter, longer, heavier, lighter)
  • Hot flashes and night sweats
  • Sleep disturbances
  • Mood changes and irritability
  • Vaginal dryness
  • Changes in libido
  • Brain fog or difficulty concentrating
  • Joint pain or stiffness

Finding Comfort

  • Stay cool: dress in layers, use fans, keep cold water nearby
  • Stay active: regular exercise can help with mood and sleep
  • Eat well: focus on calcium, vitamin D, and balanced nutrition
  • Sleep hygiene: maintain a consistent sleep schedule
  • Talk about it: share your experience with trusted people

When to Seek Support

If symptoms significantly affect your quality of life, speak with a healthcare provider about management options. You don't have to simply endure severe symptoms.

title: When to Seek Medical Help
summary: A clear guide on symptoms and situations that warrant a visit to a healthcare provider.
content:
Signs You Should See a Provider

While many cycle variations are normal, certain symptoms may need medical attention. Consider making an appointment if you experience:

Urgent Signs

  • Extremely heavy bleeding (soaking through a pad/tampon every hour)
  • Severe pelvic pain that doesn't improve with over-the-counter pain relief
  • Fever with pelvic pain
  • Sudden, severe abdominal pain

Worth Discussing

  • Periods consistently lasting more than 7 days
  • Cycles shorter than 21 days or longer than 35 days
  • Missing 3 or more periods in a row (if not pregnant)
  • Significant changes in your usual pattern
  • Bleeding after menopause
  • Pain that interferes with daily activities
  • New or unusual discharge with odor

How to Prepare for Your Visit

  1. Bring your cycle tracking data (Bloom logs can help!)
  2. Note when symptoms started and how often they occur
  3. List any medications or supplements you take
  4. Write down your questions beforehand

title: Sexual Health & Birth Control Basics
summary: An overview of sexual health essentials and common birth control methods available in Jamaica.
content:
Understanding Your Options

There are many birth control methods available, each with different effectiveness rates and considerations. Here's a brief overview:

Barrier Methods

  • Condoms (external/internal): Also protect against STIs. 85-98% effective with proper use.
  • Diaphragm: Used with spermicide. Requires fitting by a provider.

Hormonal Methods

  • Birth control pills: Taken daily. 91-99% effective.
  • Injectable (Depo-Provera): Every 3 months. 94-99% effective.
  • Implant: Placed under the skin. Lasts up to 3 years. 99%+ effective.
  • Hormonal IUD: Placed in the uterus. Lasts 3-7 years. 99%+ effective.

Non-Hormonal Methods

  • Copper IUD: Lasts up to 10 years. 99%+ effective.
  • Fertility awareness methods: Tracking your cycle to identify fertile days. Requires careful tracking.

STI Prevention

Condoms are the only method that protect against both pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections. Regular STI screening is recommended for sexually active individuals.

Making a Choice

The best method is one that fits your lifestyle and health needs. Discuss options with a healthcare provider to find what works for you.
